deep.reconstruction:
Context: this page belongs to a deductive sequence of numbered theorems (Lehrsätze) in elementary geometry. The facing page (next page in the bundle) contains Satz 5: no angle of a triangle can EQUAL the exterior (adjacent supplementary) angle at another vertex. That proof also cites Satz 2 (base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal), Satz 3 (the converse) and Satz 4 (a triangle cannot have two right angles). Satz 5 is proved by intersecting a line with a sphere (Kugelfläche) about A. This page proves Satz 6, the inequality half.

Theorem 6 (Lehrsatz 6). In triangle ABC, extend CB beyond B to a point D. Then angle ACB cannot exceed the exterior angle ABD. In words: no angle of a triangle exceeds the adjacent supplement (Nebenwinkel) of another of its angles.

Proof as written, with my additions in brackets.
1. Take the circular cone surface with vertex C, axis the ray CB, and half-opening angle equal to angle ABD. [It is the locus of points X with angle XCB = ABD.]
2. Suppose angle ABD < angle ACB. By the definition of the cone, the ray CA then lies outside the cone, since it makes a larger angle with the axis than the generators do. B lies on the axis, so it is inside the cone.
3. Hence the segment AB, joining an outside point to an inside point, must meet the cone surface at some point E. [This tacitly uses a continuity/separation property of the solid cone.]
4. Since E lies on the cone, angle ECB = ABD. [Since E lies on segment BA, ray BE = ray BA, so angle EBD = ABD.] Hence angle ECB = angle EBD.
5. So in triangle EBC, the angle at C equals the exterior angle at B (D lies on CB extended beyond B). This contradicts Satz 5.
6. [The case ABD = ACB is excluded directly by Satz 5.] Therefore ACB ≤ ABD and indeed ACB < ABD.

What it serves: Euclid I.16, the exterior angle theorem, proved without the parallel postulate (absolute/neutral geometry). Instead of Euclid's midpoint-and-doubling construction, the method intersects lines with surfaces of revolution (sphere, cone). This fits Gauss's documented interest in the foundations of geometry and the independence of the parallel axiom.
errors: No substantive error. Unstated assumptions: (a) a segment from a point outside the solid cone to a point inside it meets the cone surface (a continuity/convexity axiom, analogous to the line–sphere intersection used in Satz 5); (b) E ≠ B and E lies on segment AB, so ray BE = ray BA and EBD = ABD; (c) triangle EBC is nondegenerate, since E is not on line CB.
Only the strict case ABD < ACB is treated explicitly; equality is covered by Satz 5, which is what makes 'cannot be greater' amount to the full statement ACB < ABD.

Using a spatial cone for a planar theorem is logically unnecessary: its trace in plane ABC is just the ray from C making angle ABD with CB. It is consistent, though, with the sphere-based method of Satz 5.

results.what: In any triangle, an interior angle is less than the exterior angle at another vertex (Lehrsatz 6), proved by contradiction using an auxiliary cone and the equality case (Satz 5)
results.modern_name: Exterior angle theorem (Euclid Elements I.16), valid in neutral/absolute geometry
results.usually_credited_to: Euclid (c. 300 BC); neutral-geometry status emphasized by Saccheri, Legendre, Bolyai, Lobachevsky

results.what: Proof method replacing Euclid's construction by intersecting a line with a sphere/cone about a vertex (spatial auxiliary loci, continuity)
results.modern_name: Alternative proof of I.16 via loci/continuity in absolute geometry

deep.surprise_reason: The result is classical (Euclid I.16), and Gauss's interest in the foundations of geometry is well known. The mildly unusual feature is the proof style: an auxiliary cone surface, with Satz 5 proved via a sphere, instead of Euclid's construction. It is a minor unpublished foundational detail, not a new theorem.
